questions.question: What is the limit of the sequence below as n→∞?

moves.name: Recognize the definition of e
moves.professor: That's the engine of continuous growth—e itself. Perfect form recognition.

moves.name: Take the logarithm and use L'Hôpital's Rule
moves.professor: That'll get you there, but it's a siege when a single strike would do.

moves.name: Plug in n=∞ directly: 1^∞ = 1
moves.professor: 1^∞ is a mask for an indeterminate form. Don't be fooled by appearances.

questions.question: Determine the best first step to test convergence of the series below.

moves.name: Compare with 1/n^2
moves.professor: 1/n^2 is the dominant force; comparison cuts straight to convergence.

moves.name: Compare with 1/n
moves.professor: Your comparison points the wrong way—1/n diverges but the series is smaller. No conclusion.

moves.name: Apply the Integral Test
moves.professor: Works, but it's heavy armor for a skirmish. Direct comparison is swifter.

questions.question: Does the improper integral converge or diverge?

moves.name: Converges by p-integral (p=1/2 < 1)
moves.professor: Finite endpoint with p<1 means safe landing. The singularity is tame.

moves.name: Diverges because of the vertical asymptote at 0
moves.professor: An asymptote doesn't guarantee divergence—check the exponent. p<1 converges near zero.

moves.name: Use limit comparison with 1/x
moves.professor: Acceptable, but the p-test is the sharper arrow.

questions.question: Can the Integral Test be applied directly to the series below?

moves.name: No, the function is not eventually decreasing
moves.professor: Integral Test demands a steady downward slope; cos² oscillates too wildly.

moves.name: Yes, compare the integral to 1/x
moves.professor: You can't just force a non-monotone function into the Integral Test mold. Wrong weapon.

moves.name: Apply the Ratio Test instead
moves.professor: Ratio Test is also ineffective here, but at least you're reaching for a valid tool. Still a struggle.

questions.question: What is the most efficient test for the series below?

moves.name: Geometric series test, r=2/3 < 1
moves.professor: One glance at the common ratio and victory is yours. Clean geometric strike.

moves.name: Ratio Test
moves.professor: Ratio Test works, but it's like using a siege engine on an open gate.

moves.name: Divergence Test: terms go to 0, so series diverges
moves.professor: Terms going to 0 is the starting line, not the finish. Divergence Test can't prove convergence.

questions.question: Identify the quickest valid argument that the series below diverges.

moves.name: p-series with p=1 diverges
moves.professor: The harmonic series is the classic p=1 trap. One word: diverges.

moves.name: Integral Test with ∫1/x dx
moves.professor: Solid, though slower than invoking the p-series rule directly.

moves.name: Limit comparison with 1/n^2 gives limit ∞, so diverges
moves.professor: Limit ∞ means the comparison is inconclusive—you can't force divergence from a convergent series.

questions.question: Determine if the sequence converges or diverges.

moves.name: Diverges; terms oscillate among 1, 0, -1
moves.professor: No settling down—three values cycle forever. Divergent and proud of it.

moves.name: Converges to 0 because sine is bounded
moves.professor: Boundedness isn't enough; the sequence must approach a single value. It bounces instead.

moves.name: Squeeze Theorem with -1 ≤ sin ≤ 1
moves.professor: Squeeze only works if the outer bounds converge to the same limit. They don't here—dodged, but not a solution.

questions.question: Choose the best comparison to determine convergence of the improper integral.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^2
moves.professor: For large x, √(x²-1) ~ x, so integrand ~ 1/x². That's the kill shot.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x
moves.professor: 1/x is too big and diverges, but your target is smaller—no conclusion. Wrong target.

moves.name: Trig substitution x = sec θ
moves.professor: It works, but why unsheathe a heavy blade when a simple comparison ends it?

questions.question: True or False: If lim_{n→∞} a_n = 0, then Σ a_n converges.

moves.name: False; the harmonic series is a counterexample
moves.professor: Necessary but not sufficient. The harmonic series is the classic ambush.

moves.name: True; vanishing terms guarantee convergence
moves.professor: That's the most common pitfall in all of series. Terms must vanish, but not fast enough sometimes.

questions.question: Find the sum of the convergent series.

moves.name: Sum = 9, first term 0.9, ratio 0.9
moves.professor: Sharp eye—starting at n=1 shifts the sum. The formula yields 9.

moves.name: Sum = 10, using 1/(1-0.9)
moves.professor: You forgot the index starts at 1, not 0. That slip costs the battle.

moves.name: Sum = 1/(1-0.9) - 1 = 9
moves.professor: Correct adjustment, but you took the longer path. Direct a/(1-r) with a=0.9 is faster.

questions.question: Why does the Integral Test fail for the series below?

moves.name: The terms are not positive
moves.professor: Integral Test requires a nonnegative function. Alternating signs break the contract.

moves.name: The function is not continuous
moves.professor: Continuous extension exists, but that's not the real issue. The positivity condition is the first line.

moves.name: The absolute values decrease; test applies
moves.professor: Decreasing absolute value doesn't rescue positivity. The test is strictly for nonnegative terms.

questions.question: Explain why the integral below is not zero despite the integrand being odd.

moves.name: The improper integral diverges due to a non-integrable singularity at 0
moves.professor: Symmetry doesn't save you when the function blows up in the middle. Divergence wins.

moves.name: By odd symmetry, the integral must be zero
moves.professor: Odd symmetry only applies if the integral converges. Here it diverges—a classic pitfall.

moves.name: Use Cauchy principal value to assign 0
moves.professor: CPV gives 0 but the improper integral itself diverges. You sidestep the issue without solving it.

questions.question: A sequence is increasing and bounded above. What can be concluded?

moves.name: It converges, by the Monotone Convergence Theorem
moves.professor: Monotone bounded sequences are guaranteed to converge. Solid foundation.

moves.name: It necessarily diverges to infinity
moves.professor: Bounded above means it can't escape to infinity. It must settle somewhere finite.

moves.name: More information is needed
moves.professor: The theorem gives you certainty—no extra info required. Trust the axioms.

questions.question: Determine convergence/divergence of the series by the quickest method.

moves.name: Diverges by Divergence Test; limit is 1 ≠ 0
moves.professor: The terms walk stubbornly toward 1. Divergence Test ends it instantly.

moves.name: Compare with harmonic series, n/(n+1) ≥ 1/2
moves.professor: Valid, but why wield a comparison when the limit not zero already condemns it?

moves.name: Integral Test
moves.professor: The Integral Test here is like drawing a map when the destination is right in front of you.

questions.question: True or False: Σ 1/n^p converges for any p > 1, no matter how close p is to 1.

moves.name: True; p > 1 guarantees convergence
moves.professor: Even p=1.0001 brings convergence. The p=1 boundary is a razor's edge.

moves.name: False; p must be significantly larger than 1, like p≥2
moves.professor: Any p>1, no matter how tiny the margin, tips the scale. Remember that.

questions.question: If 0 ≤ a_n ≤ b_n and Σ b_n converges, what can be said about Σ a_n?

moves.name: Σ a_n converges by Comparison Test
moves.professor: Smaller than a convergent series? Safe and sound. Comparison Test seals it.

moves.name: Σ a_n diverges because it is smaller
moves.professor: Being smaller than a convergent series is a haven, not a hazard. Direction matters.

moves.name: No conclusion without more information
moves.professor: The Comparison Test directly gives convergence. Hesitation here costs momentum.

questions.question: Which approach best determines convergence of the improper integral?

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^{3/2} for large x
moves.professor: ln x grows slower than any power, so 1/x^{2-ε} dominates. Sharp comparison.

moves.name: Use integration by parts
moves.professor: You'll reach an answer, but it's a grind. Comparison breaks through faster.

moves.name: Apply the p-integral rule directly
moves.professor: ln x in the numerator breaks the pure p-integral form. Can't apply blindly.

questions.question: For which x does the geometric series Σ x^n converge?

moves.name: |x| < 1
moves.professor: The golden interval. Outside, it's chaos. Geometric series has no mercy for |x|≥1.

moves.name: x < 1
moves.professor: What about x=-2? Negative values matter. Absolute value is the key.

moves.name: All real x
moves.professor: If only. The series explodes outside the unit interval.

questions.question: Find the limit of the sequence.

moves.name: 0; log grows slower than any positive power
moves.professor: Growth hierarchy: powers beat logs every time. Zero it is.

moves.name: 1; because ln n and n both go to infinity
moves.professor: n crushes ln n. Tendency to infinity doesn't mean ratio one. Watch the speeds.

moves.name: Use L'Hôpital's Rule on (ln n)/n
moves.professor: Elegant, and confirms the limit 0. Growth intuition is faster, but the rule backs it up.

questions.question: Determine whether the series converges or diverges.

moves.name: Diverges by Integral Test; ∫ dx/(x ln x) = ln(ln x) → ∞
moves.professor: Integral Test exposes the subtle divergence. The double logarithm grows unbounded.

moves.name: Converges by Comparison Test with 1/n^2
moves.professor: 1/(n ln n) is larger than 1/n^2 for large n—comparison goes the wrong way. Misstep.

moves.name: Converges because terms go to 0
moves.professor: Vanishing terms deceived you again. This series diverges slowly but surely.
